articles.title: Same MCP version, different tools: what two independent captures revealed
articles.excerpt: Nine write tools appeared in our capture of mongodb-mcp-server that were absent from another observer's capture of the same version. The launch commands explained it: our sandbox started the server ba…
articles.body: Nine write tools appeared in our capture of mongodb-mcp-server that were absent from another observer's capture of the same version. The launch commands explained it: our sandbox started the server bare; the other capture used --readOnly and a connection string. We run HISTOR , a public log of MCP tool definitions. Paraphern maintains RugSnare , which records and compares tool contracts across releases. On 26 October, we compared the overlapping parts of our records. Some differences described the servers' launch conditions. Others exposed mistakes in the measurement process, including gaps in ours. What we actually compared The overlap contained 26 packages. HISTOR held tool lists for 21 of them. RugSnare's pins supplied 34 version captures that could be compared against our record.

articles.title: Claude Code Plan Mode: How It Works, How to Use It, and When to Skip It
articles.excerpt: Claude Code Plan Mode: How It Works, How to Use It, and When to Skip It The most expensive Claude Code mistake I know is not a bad edit. It is a confident edit. You ask for a refactor, the agent picks…
articles.body: Claude Code Plan Mode: How It Works, How to Use It, and When to Skip It The most expensive Claude Code mistake I know is not a bad edit. It is a confident edit. You ask for a refactor, the agent picks an approach in about four seconds, and twenty minutes later you are reading a diff across twelve files that solves a slightly different problem than the one you had. Nothing is broken. It is just wrong, and the cost of finding that out is the whole diff. Plan mode is the fix for that, and it costs almost nothing. Claude reads your code, writes down what it intends to do, and waits. You read the plan, change it if it is off, and only then does anything get edited.

articles.title: Svelte Explained: The Framework That Disappears
articles.excerpt: Introduction React, Vue, and Angular all work the same way at runtime: they ship a framework to the browser, which watches your data and updates the page. Svelte takes a radically different approach —…
articles.body: Introduction React, Vue, and Angular all work the same way at runtime: they ship a framework to the browser, which watches your data and updates the page. Svelte takes a radically different approach — it is a compiler. It turns your components into plain JavaScript at build time, and ships no framework at all. The result: smaller bundles, faster pages, and code that reads almost like plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Reactivity without ceremony In React you need hooks and state setters; in Svelte, reactivity is just assignment. Change a variable, and the page updates: <script> let count = 0 ; </script> <button on:click= {() = > count += 1}> Clicked {count} times </button> There is no useState, no setter function, no virtual DOM diffing.
articles.author: The Practical Developer

articles.title: Why Your Laptop Still Loses Battery Through a USB-C Hub
articles.excerpt: I work on the manufacturing side of USB-C hubs, and there is one complaint that comes back so consistently that it is worth explaining properly: the laptop is plugged in, through a 100 watt hub, and t…
articles.body: I work on the manufacturing side of USB-C hubs, and there is one complaint that comes back so consistently that it is worth explaining properly: the laptop is plugged in, through a 100 watt hub, and the battery is still going down. The hub is not lying to you. It is keeping some of the power for itself, and it is doing that because it has to. Here is the arithmetic. A hub advertising 100 watt passthrough takes 100 watts in from your charger. It then reserves somewhere between 12 and 20 watts to run its own electronics, to convert the DisplayPort signal into HDMI, and to power the peripherals you plug into it. What it passes through to the laptop is the remainder, and that is why the honest products print a second number, usually 85 watts or 87 watts, lower down on the page.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Between Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1 and 2 , the boundary separating the physical present from the echoes of the past feels uniquely thin. In software engineering, we routinely discard architectures, deprecate protocols, and terminate processes—yet their ghosts linger in unlinked disk sectors, old magnetic tapes, and our collective memories. To honor this theme, I created NecroShell : an interactive, retro-cybernetic workstation that transforms your browser into a haunted phosphor CRT terminal powered by open-source AI.

Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden Explanation: Sometimes it’s night on the ground but day in the air. As the Earth rotates to eclipse the Sun, sunset rises up from the ground. articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.
